strengths: The paper addresses a significant and timely problem: how pre-trained priors / Internet knowledge memorization cause state-of-the-art vision-language models (VLMs) to fail on standard visual perception and counting tasks.

Unlike prior visual hallucination and counterfactual benchmarks (e.g., PhD, VLind-Bench, HallusionBench) that explicitly inject biased framing into text prompts (e.g., 'Is the mouse smaller than the cat?'), this benchmark uses neutral, objective prompts (e.g., 'How many legs does this animal have?') to rigorously isolate visual bias.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering 7 distinct domains (animals, logos, flags, chess pieces, game boards, optical illusions, and patterned grids) across recent leading models (Gemini-2.5 Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4.1, o3, o4-mini).
Well-designed control experiments and analyses, including sanity checks on unmodified images, adversarial in-image text injection, and debiasing/double-checking prompt strategies.
weaknesses: Confounding factors between counting ability and prior bias: Prior work (e.g., 'Vision language models are blind', Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 2024) has shown that VLMs struggle fundamentally with low-level counting and grid tasks even without semantic priors. Disentangling raw visual counting/acuity limitations from knowledge-induced prior bias requires clearer neutral control baselines (e.g., counting unfamiliar/abstract items of identical size and complexity).

Dataset scale and diversity remain relatively modest in several categories (e.g., only 5 specific brand logos across cars and shoes, 84 game board images), which may limit broad generalizability across fine-grained visual categories.

Evaluation relies entirely on closed-source proprietary API models (Gemini-2.5, Claude 3.7, GPT-4.1, o3/o4-mini) at temperature=1.0. Including open-weight models (e.g., Qwen2-VL, LLaVA-NeXT) would significantly enhance reproducibility and allow deeper mechanistic investigation into feature representations (e.g., probing visual encoder tokens vs. language decoder activations).

strengths: Compelling and timely investigation: The paper systematically demonstrates a critical vulnerability in current frontier vision-language models—namely, that visual/textual semantic priors heavily override direct visual perception on objective tasks.

Methodological improvement over existing benchmarks: Unlike prior works (e.g., HallusionBench, VLind-Bench) that relied on leading, linguistically biased Yes/No prompts, this work uses neutral, objective visual counting and identification prompts, isolating the effect of visual and memorized semantic priors.

Comprehensive domain coverage and sanity controls: Evaluates 7 distinct domains spanning photo-realistic and abstract graphics. The inclusion of sanity checks on unmodified images (achieving 100% accuracy) convincingly shows that models possess the underlying conceptual knowledge, confirming that failures on counterfactuals stem from bias rather than ignorance.

Evaluation on state-of-the-art models: Testing frontier models including reasoning/thinking architectures (OpenAI o3, o4-mini, Gemini-2.5 Pro) and non-thinking models (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4.1) reveals that test-time compute/reasoning does not meaningfully alleviate this perceptual bias.

Careful experimental ablations: The experiments examining in-image adversarial text injection, resolution sensitivity, and prompt-based mitigation (explicit debiasing instructions and double-checking) add significant depth to the empirical findings.
weaknesses: Conflation between semantic bias and basic visual acuity/counting limitations: VLMs are well known to struggle with fine-grained counting and high-frequency visual details regardless of familiarity (as highlighted in prior work like BlindTest). While the sanity checks and error distributions suggest a strong bias towards canonical counts, the paper does not fully isolate perceptual limitations (e.g., by comparing counterfactual logos/animals directly against visually matched, unfamiliar novel geometric controls with the exact same visual dimensions and contrast).

Exclusively closed-source API evaluation: The study evaluates only proprietary models behind APIs. Evaluating open-weights models (such as Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2.5, or LLaVA-OneVision) would have allowed for deeper mechanistic analysis, such as examining whether the vision encoder actually preserves the anomaly or whether attention/logits in early language layers override the visual tokens.

Modest benchmark size and domain depth: With ~1,392 images across 7 tasks and relatively few distinct entities per domain (e.g., 5 brand logos, 20 flags), the dataset is somewhat limited in scale, even though manual quality verification is commendable.

Limited exploration of mitigations: Beyond zero-shot debiasing prompts and two-turn double-checking (which yield negligible gains), the paper does not explore more advanced interventions such as visual cropping/zooming, chain-of-thought with visual bounding/pointing, or fine-tuning approaches.

strengths: Compelling and important research question: The paper cleanly decouples visual bias from textual prompt bias. Prior counterfactual/hallucination benchmarks often embed biased assertions directly into Yes/No prompts, confounding text-only priors with multimodal interaction. Using neutral, objective counting and identification prompts cleanly exposes the models' failure to prioritize visual input over internal semantic priors.

Extensive and diverse dataset curation: The benchmark covers 7 distinct domains spanning photo-realistic images (animals, logos) and vector/abstract visual patterns (flags, chess positions, board games, optical illusions, patterned grids). The inclusion of synthetic patterned grids serves as an effective control to isolate local anomaly detection from internet-memorized concepts.

Evaluation on frontier multimodal models: The paper tests the most recent proprietary SOTA models, including both reasoning/thinking models (Gemini-2.5 Pro, o3, o4-mini) and non-thinking models (Sonnet-3.7, GPT-4.1), providing timely and relevant findings.

Thorough empirical diagnostics: Beyond raw accuracy, the paper analyzes the bias-alignment of errors (showing 75.7% of errors directly match the canonical prior), runs baseline sanity checks on unmodified images (verifying 100% recognition), tests adversarial in-image text perturbations, and evaluates prompting mitigations (debiasing and multi-turn double-checking).
weaknesses: Confounding between visual acuity/counting capacity and semantic bias: For several domains (e.g., small car emblems on full vehicles, dense stripes, Go boards), standard VLMs are known to suffer from low-level visual perception and counting limitations regardless of prior knowledge (as highlighted in prior work such as BlindTest). While the high sanity-check accuracy on canonical images partially addresses this, canonical images can be answered correctly via semantic memorization alone without requiring the model to actually count. Further controls (e.g., counting elements of random, unfamiliar objects of comparable scale) would help isolate perceptual resolution limits from bias.

Lack of open-source models and mechanistic probing: All evaluated models are closed-source proprietary APIs. Including open-weight models (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-OneVision) would permit internal representation probing (e.g., analyzing vision encoder embeddings vs. LLM cross-attention) to directly verify whether the vision encoder captures the anomaly or if the language decoder suppresses it.

Limited exploration of effective mitigation strategies: The tested debiasing techniques are restricted to zero-shot text instructions and simple double-checking turns, which show minimal improvement (+1.8% to +2.7%). Testing programmatic visual cropping/zooming or chain-of-thought bounding box grounding would provide constructive insights into how these biases can be bypassed.

strengths: Compelling and timely topic: The paper systematically investigates a critical vulnerability in state-of-the-art vision-language models—specifically how strong parametric priors (e.g., typical leg counts, iconic brand logos, standard chess setups) override visual sensory evidence during objective visual tasks like counting.

Careful experimental isolation of visual bias: Unlike prior counterfactual benchmarks that use biased or adversarial leading questions (e.g., 'Is the cat bigger than the mouse?'), this work utilizes neutral, objective counting and identification prompts, demonstrating that the failure stems from visual contextual triggers and internal priors rather than linguistic priming.

Insightful mechanistic and diagnostic analysis: The linear probing experiment on the SigLIP vision encoder vs. LLaVA-OneVision is particularly illuminating, proving that the vision representations retain high-fidelity anomaly information (95.26% accuracy), but the language model decoder actively suppresses it with memorized priors (99.43% bias rate).

Rich and rigorous analysis: The authors provide extensive ablations and investigations, including the role of background cues (LangSAM removal), test-time reasoning dynamics (reasoning token scaling and overthinking phenomena), few-shot resistance, resolution invariance, and human baseline studies under strict time constraints (0.2s–2.0s).

Broad evaluation across frontier models: The evaluation covers modern reasoning and non-reasoning frontier models (Gemini-2.5 Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4.1, o3, o4-mini, GPT-5, Grok-4) as well as open-weight and pointing models (Molmo, Moondream, Qwen2.5-VL, Pixtral).
weaknesses: Potential visual generation artifacts: Tasks involving photorealistic animals and logos rely on diffusion/generative model edits (Gemini-2.0 Flash / GPT-4o). Even with manual human filtering, subtle blending artifacts or unnatural anatomical junctions might disproportionately degrade attention in VLMs compared to native natural images.

Conflation in optical illusion evaluation: Task 6 evaluates classic optical illusions where human perceptual systems are also deceived. While the authors distinguish original and modified variants, classifying optical illusions under the same 'prior knowledge memorization' umbrella as animal leg counts introduces some conceptual ambiguity between visual perception errors and semantic knowledge priors.

Diagnostic rather than algorithmic contribution: The paper is primarily an empirical diagnostic and benchmarking paper. While the analysis is thorough, it does not propose or evaluate novel decoding-time interventions (e.g., visual contrastive decoding, attention-steering, or decoding priors penalty) to actively mitigate the problem.

strengths: Clean isolation of visual bias from textual prompt bias: Unlike existing benchmarks that rely on leading or adversarial phrasing (e.g., 'Is the mouse smaller than the cat?'), VLMBias evaluates models using neutral, objective counting and identification questions ('How many legs does this animal have?'). This clearly isolates the failure mode as language priors overriding visual perception.

Comprehensive coverage across diverse domains: The benchmark spans 7 domains (animals, brand logos, national flags, chess pieces, game boards, optical illusions, and synthetic patterned grids), covering both photorealistic generation and programmatic rendering across multiple image resolutions.

Insightful mechanistic and diagnostic investigations: The linear probing experiment on SigLIP features (Section A.8) is particularly compelling, demonstrating that visual encoders represent the counterfactual details with >95% accuracy, but the downstream language model overrides visual evidence with memorized priors.

Rigorously designed human baseline: The time-constrained human evaluation (0.2s to 2.0s exposure) convincingly demonstrates that the counterfactual images are not visually ambiguous or artifact-ridden, validating the visual ground truth.

Rich behavioral analysis: The paper provides fascinating analyses on reasoning models (e.g., overthinking leading to accuracy degradation, model overconfidence bypassing tool calls, and models actively rationalizing away counterfactual labels during few-shot prompting).
weaknesses: Potential conflation between dense counting weakness and knowledge bias: Modern VLMs are known to struggle with dense counting tasks in general (e.g., on game boards, grids, and chess pieces) even in neutral contexts. While the 100% score on unmodified images shows recognition of canonical setups, this could itself be memorization of the canonical count rather than genuine counting ability. Testing on arbitrary non-canonical configurations (without specific iconic priors) as an additional baseline would further disambiguate general counting limitations from prior-bias.

Limited variety within certain categories: Although the total image count is respectable (1,392 counterfactuals), some high-profile categories rely on a very small set of base entities (e.g., only 5 commercial logos and 4 game board types).

Limited exploration of algorithmic mitigations: While the paper diagnoses why prompting, double-checking, and few-shot examples fail, and highlights that specialized pointing models perform better, it does not explore architectural or decoding-time intervention strategies (e.g., contrastive decoding, attention re-weighting, or visual grounding regularization) to help general-purpose VLMs overcome these biases.

strengths: Compelling and rigorous experimental setup: Unlike previous bias/hallucination benchmarks that embed leading or biased statements within the textual prompt (e.g., 'Is the mouse bigger than the cat?'), this work evaluates models with neutral, objective questions (e.g., direct counting), cleanly isolating whether failures are driven by textual priming or genuine prior visual knowledge overriding visual perception.

Comprehensive coverage and taxonomy: The benchmark evaluates seven diverse domains ranging from natural images (animals with extra legs, modified brand logos) to programmatically generated abstract domains (chessboards, game boards, flags, optical illusions, and novel patterned grids), preventing domain-specific overfitting of conclusions.

Deep mechanistic diagnostics: The paper goes well beyond leaderboard reporting by providing insightful analytical experiments: (1) linear probing of frozen vision encoder representations (SigLIP) showing that visual features successfully distinguish anomalous counts (95.26%), confirming the LLM backbone overrides visual evidence; (2) background removal ablation showing that context cues strongly trigger the bias; (3) test-time compute analysis revealing an inverted-U relationship where excessive thinking tokens lead to overthinking and degradation; and (4) evaluation of pointing/grounding models showing that explicit spatial localization significantly mitigates bias.

Solid baselines and controls: Includes a thorough sanity check on unmodified images (confirming 100% accuracy on original subjects), resolution sensitivity tests, repeated-run stability checks, and a time-controlled human study demonstrating that the counterfactual images are visually unambiguous to human observers.
weaknesses: Primarily diagnostic without a novel algorithmic mitigation: While the paper evaluates existing mitigations (prompt debiasing, few-shot prompting, code/tool use, pointing models), it does not propose a novel architectural or algorithmic technique to prevent language priors from overriding visual tokens during decoding.

Potential conflation of counting limitations with prior bias: General-purpose VLMs are notoriously weak at dense visual counting even in neutral settings. Although the authors carefully measure the bias-alignment rate (showing ~75.7% of errors directly match canonical priors) and report 100% accuracy on unmodified base images, some tasks (e.g., Sudoku/Go board line counting or small car emblems) inherently challenge standard patch resolutions and spatial attention mechanisms independent of prior knowledge.

Modest benchmark size: The core benchmark comprises 1,392 counterfactual images across seven tasks. While manually curated and verified to ensure high visual quality, expanding the test suite further would strengthen the statistical power across finer subcategories.
